Buddhigt writings, whether Indian or foreign, are 'divided into three classes, technically called the Tripithaka or "the three reposition sries." The first of these comprises the sayings of Buddha himself (Satra), and as such, constitutes the corner-stone of Buddhism Upon it were founded the Buddhist systems of: philosophy (Abhidharma) and ethics (Vinaya). Tha works* included under these three heads are, however, of very unequal merit, and held in very different estimation by their followers. Nor has the principle of the triple division been very strictly adhered to, for there are now many works of such a miscellaneous character, that they may be included under all the three:divisions It is evidently on this account that the Nepalese and the Tibetan Buddhists have adopted other and more comprehensive classifications. The religious literature of the Tibetans is comprised in the great collection called the Kahgyur, and that is divided, for facility of reference, into seven classes, each of which includes a variety of works of unequal merit and extent. 'Tha, first class is called Dulva or discipline; the 2nd, Sherch'hin or metzphysics ; 3rd, Phalch'hin or rules of the religious community ; 4th, Dhomseks, miscellaneous doctrines; 5th, Do-de, aphorisms or sayings of Buddha; 6th, Nyangdag, or final deliverance; ant 7१५ Gyut or mystical doctrine.
